ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: bedroom
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A private room of about 5x5 with a real floor, a light and some decoration
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Every colonist wakes up in their bedroom, and the mood from it lasts the whole day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists wake up each morning with a mood thought based on how impressive their bedroom is. A private room of about 5x5 with a real floor, a light and a plant or sculpture is the cheapest lasting mood bonus you can build, so give each colonist their own room as soon as you have the wood. Size matters more than it seems, because every piece of furniture takes up some of the room's space.

li.heading: How big to build
li.text: Space is 1.4 per floor tile, minus 0.9 for every tile blocked by furniture, and a good bedroom has 25 or more. With a single bed and a dresser inside, the common sizes come out like this:
li.after: Once furnished, a 3x4 or smaller reads "cramped" and a 3x6 or 4x5 reads "rather tight". The bedroom plan comes in four sizes: cozy (3x4), the budget option until you can afford more, standard (5x5), roomy (6x6), and a sleeping hut (4x4) for tribal colonies.

li.heading: Raising the mood
li.text:
Bedroom impressiveness under 20 costs -2 mood. From 30 to 39 it gives +1, at 85 or more ("very impressive") +5, and at 240 or more +8. Fix the weakest room stat first: a real floor, a light and a plant pot usually do more than an expensive bed.
With Royalty, nobles from Knight or Dame upward need an end table and a dresser in their bedroom.

li.heading: When it stops being a bedroom
li.text: A room stops counting as a bedroom if it holds a medical or prisoner bed, or more than one unassigned bed. A room with a child assigned also needs a parent assigned. Couples want a double bed in a shared room; the couple's bedroom plan is laid out for them.

li.heading: Placement and temperature
li.text: Group bedrooms near the dining and rec rooms, away from the kitchen, butcher room and crematorium. Heat them in winter and cool them in summer: sleeping on the ground, outside, in the cold or in the heat costs -4 mood each, for a day. Without power, torch lamps give light, a campfire gives heat and a passive cooler takes the edge off summer.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: barracks
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Shared sleeping quarters: cheap and quick early on, a drag on mood later
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A barracks gets you through the first winter. Start on private rooms before the second.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A barracks is any room with two or more ordinary beds that isn't a valid bedroom. Everyone sleeping there shares one impressiveness score, so one big, clean, decorated room serves every sleeper for the price of one set of decoration. It's a solid start, but people walking past wake the sleepers, and most experienced players move colonists into private rooms as soon as they can.

li.heading: One room, one score
li.text:
Two or more ordinary beds make a barracks. It stops counting if it holds a prisoner bed or qualifies as a bedroom, so never put a prisoner or medical bed in it.
Every sleeper's mood thought comes from the room's single score. Blood on the floor counts against all of them, and a good floor, lights and a sculpture count for all of them, so spend on those first. A 7x7 room with 4 beds and 4 end tables has about 57.8 space, which reads "somewhat spacious".

li.heading: Who should sleep there
li.text:
When someone walks past a sleeping colonist, the sleeper gets disturbed sleep: -1 mood for a day. Keep the barracks off the main corridors so nobody walks past the beds at night.
The exact mood penalty for sleeping in a shared room isn't confirmed, but community guides agree that private rooms are better. Use the barracks for the first weeks, for new arrivals and for soldiers, then move people into bedrooms. A soldiers' barracks belongs near the armory and the dining room.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dining room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Tables, enough chairs and a clean, pretty room right next to the kitchen
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Everyone eats here every day, so decoration in the dining room reaches the whole colony.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist eats here once or twice a day, so a dining room repays decoration faster than almost any other room, and it gets its own impressiveness mood bonus. Give it a wall and a door in common with the kitchen so meals don't travel across the base, and keep the butcher room, blood and bodies well away. The dining room plan seats 4, 8 or 12.

li.heading: What makes it a dining room
li.text:
Each table counts toward the dining room role. Tables come as 1x2, 2x2, 2x4 and 3x3. Keep beds and stoves out: a bed turns the room into a bedroom or barracks, and one stove (28) outscores two tables (24).
Build enough chairs for everyone who eats at the same time. Eating without a table costs -3 mood for a day.

li.heading: The mood bonus
li.text:
Dining room impressiveness gives +2 mood from 40, +5 from 85 and up to +8 from 240. Unlike a bedroom, a dull dining room costs nothing. Lights, a real floor and a sculpture raise it, and so does keeping it clean: every tile of blood is -30 beauty and -10 cleanliness.
Many colonies combine dining and recreation in one big room, so one set of decoration serves both. In a tribal colony, wooden tables and torch lamps earn the same bonus, because impressiveness doesn't depend on tech level.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: recreation room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Several kinds of recreation in one room, between dining and bedrooms
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Colonists tire of playing the same game. Give them three or four different things to do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists refill their Recreation need at recreation buildings, but they get bored of doing the same thing over and over. A rec room with several different kinds of recreation keeps the need high and gives its own impressiveness bonus. The richer your colony gets, the more variety people expect. The plan comes as a games corner, a rec room, and a recreation hall with billiards, poker, chess and a television.

li.heading: How much variety
li.text: A colonist gets bored of a recreation type above 50% tolerance and stays bored until it falls below 30%. The recommended number of kinds rises with the colony's expectations:
li.after: Mix kinds: a game table, a TV, an instrument with Royalty, and horseshoes just outside the door. Without power, horseshoes and chess still give two kinds of recreation. A hoopstone ring is the same kind as horseshoes.

li.heading: The buildings
li.after: Recreation is gained at 36% per hour times the building's multiplier: a billiards table gives 46.8% per hour, a flatscreen TV 50.4%. Bedridden patients can only watch TV, so put one in the hospital too.

li.heading: Laying it out
li.text: Put the rec room between the dining room and the bedrooms. Leave walking room between buildings, because every blocked tile costs space and impressiveness. Each recreation building adds 7 to the rec room score, against 12 per table for a dining room.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: kitchen
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A small, clean cooking room between the freezer and the dining room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Keep the kitchen floor clean and the butchering next door.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Food poisoning comes from the cook's skill and the cleanliness of the room the stove stands in, so the kitchen has to stay clean. Keep it small, give it a smooth or tiled floor, and keep butchering and through-traffic out. Put it between the freezer and the dining room so meals take the shortest trip. The plan has one stove or two, or a stove with a butchery behind an inner door, so the blood stays on the far side of a wall.

li.heading: Cleanliness and food poisoning
li.text:
Community testing suggests the dirty-room food poisoning chance stops applying once room cleanliness is about -2 or better. A butcher table lowers cleanliness by roughly 15 on its tile, which alone can make a small kitchen dirty, so butcher in a separate room next door with its own door into the freezer.
Floor the kitchen with smooth stone or tile, and with sterile tile (+0.6 cleanliness per tile) once you can afford it. Give someone a high Cleaning priority so the floor stays clean.

li.heading: Stoves, benches and doors
li.text:
A stove plus one workbench is still a kitchen; a stove with two workbenches becomes a workshop. Put a shelf for ingredients inside, a door straight into the freezer and another into the dining room, and keep the room off the main hallway.
Electric stoves work best between 10 and 35 °C and slow to 70% speed outside that range. Without power, use a fueled stove or a campfire, and keep it on stone rather than a wooden floor.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: freezer
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A double-walled, cooled room that holds food at or below 0 °C
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Check the freezer's temperature as soon as a heat wave starts.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Food doesn't spoil at all at or below 0 °C, so a freezer turns a few days of meals into months of stock. Between 0 and 10 °C food still spoils, only more slowly, and raw meat rots in 2 days unrefrigerated. Put the freezer right next to the kitchen, and haul harvests and fresh meat into it promptly. The plan comes as a small cold store with one cooler, a freezer with two and a large one with three.

points.li: Make it about 6x6, as experienced players suggest, with wall space left for extra coolers, and roof it.
Double-wall it, so the cold holds through a heat wave.
Vent the coolers' hot side outdoors, never into another roofed room.
Use two doors in a row toward the kitchen, so opening one doesn't let the warm air in.
Build one more cooler than you think you need. Coolers set to different targets, such as -5 °C and -10 °C, let one idle on low power.

li.heading: Heat waves and solar flares
li.text: A heat wave can add up to 17 °C to the outside temperature; the spare cooler and the double walls are there for those days. Coolers stop during a solar flare, so then the walls and the closed doors have to hold the cold on their own.

li.heading: Without power
li.text: Passive coolers can't go below 17 °C, so they can't keep anything frozen. Rely on pemmican, which keeps for 70 days, cook only what you need and keep raw stock small.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: butcher room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Butchering in its own small room, next to the freezer and away from the stove
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Butcher next to the freezer, so the meat goes straight in.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Butchering spreads blood, and blood near a stove raises the chance of food poisoning. A small butcher room of its own keeps the mess away from the kitchen and the dining room. Put it next to the freezer, with a short route in from the hunting grounds.

li.heading: Blood and bodies
li.text:
According to community testing, a butcher table lowers cleanliness by about 15 on its tile, and every tile of blood is -10 cleanliness and -30 beauty. A smooth stone or tiled floor lets the blood be cleaned up quickly.
Seeing a corpse costs -4 mood and a rotting one -6, each for half a day. Keep a corpse stockpile and a meat shelf inside the room or in the freezer next door, not out where people walk.

li.heading: Next to the freezer
li.text: Raw meat rots in 2 days unrefrigerated. Give the room a door straight into the freezer, and wall it off from the kitchen. In a tribal colony a butcher spot works the same way: give it its own room, away from the campfire.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: workshop
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Workbenches with walkways and materials close by, kept lit and mild
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A crafter walks to the materials for every bill. Keep them close.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A room becomes a workshop when its workbenches outscore everything else in it. Crafters spend long hours there, so light, a sensible temperature and materials close at hand pay off in faster work. Put it right beside the storeroom.

li.heading: When a room counts as a workshop
li.text: Each workbench adds 27 to the workshop score; a crafting spot adds nothing. A research bench counts for more than two workbenches, so a room with one research bench and two benches is a laboratory, and a third bench makes it a workshop again. Give the research bench a room of its own.

li.heading: Benches, shelves and heat
li.text: Line the benches along the walls, with a shelf of their materials beside each one, and put the storeroom next door. Many benches work at only 70% speed outside 10-35 °C, so keep the room lit and heat or cool it to stay in that range. Electric benches stop during a solar flare.

li.heading: Benches that need no power

points.li: Hand tailor bench
Fueled smithy
Art bench
Stonecutter's table

li.after: Keep fueled benches off wooden floors.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: smithy
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Weapons, armor and tools made on a stone floor beside the metal store
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Stone floor under the forge, wood and cloth in another room.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The smithy makes melee weapons and, later, armor and tools. The fueled version burns wood and needs no power, which makes it the main source of weapons for a medieval colony. Give it a stone floor and keep the metal store and the armory close by. The plan comes as a medieval forge, a smithy, and an armorer's workshop with a machining table beside the smithy.

li.heading: Fueled or electric
li.text: The fueled smithy is medieval tech and burns wood; the electric smithy is industrial. Smithing research costs 700, or 1,050 on a tribal start. Research it early on a tribal start despite the higher cost: it's how you get metal weapons, and the fueled smithy needs no electricity.

li.heading: Around the forge
li.text: A smithy counts as a workbench, so the room scores as a workshop. A fueled smithy on a wooden floor is a fire risk, so floor the room with stone and keep wood and cloth stockpiles in another room. Store steel and other metals next door, with the armory a short walk away, and keep the smithy lit and at a comfortable temperature for the smith.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: tailor shop
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A tailoring bench beside the cloth and leather store
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Plant the cotton in spring if you want parkas by winter.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Tailors turn cloth and leather into the clothes your colonists need for winter, summer and their mood. The bench is simple; the real limit is cloth, which takes weeks to grow. Keep the shop next to the textile store and plan the fields well ahead. The plan comes as a sewing room, a tailor's shop and a tailoring hall with two benches.

li.heading: Growing the cloth

table.li: Crop | Listed growing days | Real days (about)

li.after: Plant cotton early, and devilstrand long before you need it. Set bills to "do until you have X" so the tailor doesn't burn through your cloth.

li.heading: The shop
li.text:
The hand tailor bench is medieval and needs no power; the electric tailor bench is industrial. Either one counts as a workbench, so the room scores as a workshop.
Clothes and cloth left outdoors deteriorate, so keep cloth and leather on shelves next to the bench, indoors. Put the shop near the armory so finished parkas and armor go straight onto shelves.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: laboratory
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A quiet, clean, lit room for the research bench and nothing else
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A researcher spends whole days at the bench. Give it a quiet room of its own.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Research decides when you get electricity, hydroponics, medicine and better weapons. A research bench in its own quiet, lit, clean room keeps your researcher working steadily, and keeps the room from being counted as a workshop. Leave space to upgrade to the hi-tech bench later. The plan comes as a scholar's study for a medieval colony, a laboratory, a large laboratory, and a research wing with two hi-tech benches and a multi-analyzer.

li.heading: Keeping it a laboratory
li.text: A research bench or gene equipment makes a room a laboratory, unless three or more workbenches outscore it and turn it into a workshop. Put the lab next to the workshop, behind its own door, with a light and a real floor, and keep it clean.

li.heading: Simple and hi-tech benches
li.text:
Most industrial projects need only the simple research bench, which needs no power, so tribes can research from day one. The hi-tech research bench needs Microelectronics, and medicine production (1,500 research, 3,000 on a tribal start) needs the hi-tech bench. Leave space beside the bench for that upgrade and for add-ons such as the multi-analyzer.
With Ideology, slaves can't do research.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: hospital
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Medical beds, sterile floors, bright light and a TV, close to where fights end
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Sweep the hospital floor every day; dirt raises the infection chance.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The hospital is where wounds heal and surgery succeeds or fails. Cleanliness cuts infection and raises surgery odds, light matters at every bed, and hospital beds speed up recovery. Build it early, keep it spotless, and put it on the main corridor near where fights end, away from the freezer's cold door, so the wounded arrive fast. The hospital plan comes as an infirmary with 2 beds, rooms with 3 or 4, a ward with 9, and a surgery with a single bed.

li.heading: Infection and surgery
li.text: Room cleanliness multiplies the chance that a wound gets infected:

table.li: Where the patient lies | Infection chance
A floored room with no filth | 50%
A clean room with sterile tiles | 32%

li.after: Surgery odds fall to 75% in complete darkness at the bed's head, and as low as 60% in a filthy room. Lay sterile tile as soon as you can; until then, any smooth floor, cleaned often. Light every bed.

li.heading: Beds and monitors
li.text:
One medical bed makes the room a hospital. A prisoner bed breaks it, and a hospital that is also someone's bedroom counts as neither. Hospital bed rest effectiveness runs from 100% (normal) to 160% (legendary), and a linked vitals monitor at each bed brings tend quality to +17% and immunity gain to 1.13x, so link one to every bed.
Keep a medicine shelf inside, and add a sculpture and a TV the patients can see from their beds: bedridden patients can only watch TV for recreation.

li.heading: In a tribal colony
li.text: Set ordinary beds to medical, light them with torch lamps and keep the floor swept. Light and cleanliness affect surgery and infection whatever the bed.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: prison cell
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: One prisoner bed, one door, stone walls, and a room that isn't cramped
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Prisoners do try to escape. Build cells with stone walls and a single door.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A prison cell holds one prisoner while you recruit, convert, ransom or release them. Prisoners feel their cell's impressiveness much like a bedroom, so a cramped, ugly cell means an unhappy prisoner. Strong walls and a single door keep escape attempts rare. The prison plan comes as a cell, a furnished cell with a table to eat at, a shared cell, and a cell block of three cells off a corridor, each behind its own door.

li.heading: What a cell needs

points.li: One bed set "for prisoners", in a fully enclosed room. An ordinary bed, or more than one bed, changes that.
25 space or more, the same as a bedroom, because a prisoner's mood uses the cell's impressiveness as a bedroom would.
A light, a floor, and a table and chair so the prisoner doesn't eat off the floor.
One door, stone walls, and no door straight to the outside.

li.after: Colonists and slaves can't share a room with prisoners.

li.heading: Escapes and wardens
li.text: Security doors lengthen the time between escape attempts, and more exits shorten it. Keep the armory and any spare weapons well away from the cells, and put the cells on the warden's route, near the dining room. A nutrient paste dispenser facing into the cell can feed prisoners who can walk.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: prison barracks
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Several prisoners in one room: cheap, but every escape attempt spreads
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Keep the troublemakers in single cells and the quiet ones together.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Two or more prisoner beds in one room make a prison barracks; medical prisoner beds count too. It's cheaper than separate cells, but every prisoner rolls for escape on their own, and one break can drag nearby cells into it. Use it only for prisoners you don't expect to cause trouble.

li.heading: How a break spreads
li.text: Each prisoner rolls for escape separately, so more prisoners means more breaks, and the escape chance is multiplied by the number of exits. A prison break always involves the room it starts in, and other prison rooms within 20 tiles join it half the time. If you hold many prisoners, keep separate prison rooms more than 20 tiles apart.

li.heading: Who to keep here
li.text: Use it for low-risk prisoners waiting for ransom or release, and recruit dangerous ones from single cells. Colonists and slaves can't share the room. Give it one door, stone walls, and a table with chairs, and keep weapons and the armory far away.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: storeroom
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A roofed room full of shelves, between the workshops and the entrance
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Everything on a shelf is one less ugly pile on the floor.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Most items left outdoors slowly deteriorate, and loose piles make rooms ugly. A roofed storeroom with shelves keeps materials safe and out of sight. Put it between the workshops and the main entrance so haulers and crafters walk less. The plan comes as a store closet, a storeroom and a large storeroom.

li.heading: Why shelves
li.text: Every loose stack on the floor is -5 beauty; items on shelves don't count. Players report that shelves count as covered, so items on them don't deteriorate. Shelves make a roofed room a storeroom, at 1 point per shelf, so almost any other furniture outranks them.

li.heading: Setting it up

points.li: Roof it, floor it and line it with shelves.
Build it from stone if you can; a wooden room full of wood and cloth burns fast.
Store chemfuel and mortar shells away from everything else.
Keep a dumping stockpile outside for junk, and the main store inside.

li.after: Everything you store counts toward colony wealth, and wealth drives raid size, so sell or use surplus instead of hoarding it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: barn
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A roof, sleeping spots and stored feed for your animals, next to the hay field
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Count the animals and the hay before the first frost.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A barn gives your animals a roof, somewhere to sleep and a store of feed for the months when nothing grows. Without stored hay or kibble, herds starve in winter. Put it beside the haygrass field, inside or attached to the pen. The plan comes as a kennel, a barn, and a large barn with thirteen beds.

li.heading: Feed for winter
li.text: Hay is 0.05 nutrition per unit, and one haygrass plant yields 18 hay. Harvesting a plant triples what it is worth:

table.li: Eaten standing in the field | about 0.30

li.after: Plant haygrass next to the barn and harvest it rather than letting the animals graze it. Kibble is made 50 at a time from meat or animal products plus vegetables or hay. Stockpile hay or kibble inside the barn before winter.

li.heading: Fences, doors and warmth
li.text: Animals eat standing crops unless fenced or zoned away, so fence them off from the fields. Keep the barn warm enough for your animals in winter, and away from bedrooms. A manhunter pack breaks down a door if it sees a colonist run behind it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: greenhouse
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Hydroponics under a sun lamp: crops in any season, if the power holds
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Put batteries behind the sun lamp; a basin crop dies within hours of losing power.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A greenhouse lets you grow food through winter, toxic fallout and bad soil. Hydroponics basins grow crops very fast but need constant power, and every roofed crop needs a sun lamp. A power cut can kill the whole crop, so plan for solar flares and blackouts. The plan comes as a small greenhouse with two basins, a greenhouse with four, and a hydroponics bay with six.

li.heading: Light and power
li.text: Most plants need 51% light. Standing lamps give at most 50%, so only a sun lamp will do. One sun lamp covers up to 24 basins, so lay out 24 basins around each lamp.

table.li: Hydroponics basin | 70 W each | day and night
Sun lamp | 2,900 W | about 13 hours a day

li.after: Hydroponics basins have 280% fertility. Crops grow normally between 6 and 42 °C.

li.heading: When the power fails
li.text: If the power fails, basin plants mostly die within about 8 hours. Back the greenhouse with batteries and more than one power source. Batteries don't help during a solar flare, so harvest anything close to ripe before the basin plants start dying.

li.heading: What to grow
li.text: Grow rice or strawberries in basins. Potatoes do poorly there, so save them for poor soil outdoors. Corn, devilstrand and haygrass can't be grown in basins at all.

li.heading: Without power, or with pollution
li.text: Without power, leave up to a quarter of the room unroofed (300 tiles at most) so sunlight reaches the crops. The room still holds heat, at a higher heating cost. With Biotech, roofs and basins don't protect crops from pollution.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: crypt and graveyard
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Graves and sarcophagi out of sight of the routes people use every day
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Bury your own dead out of sight of the dining room.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Corpses lying around cost mood for everyone who walks past, and friends of the dead want them properly buried. A crypt or graveyard gives bodies somewhere to go, and with Ideology it's where funerals happen. Keep it reachable, but out of sight of the dining room and bedrooms. The plan comes as a tomb for one, a crypt for three and a catacomb for eight.

li.heading: Burying your own
li.text:
Seeing a corpse costs -4 mood and a rotting one -6, each for half a day. Dig graves or build sarcophagi in an out-of-the-way room or walled plot near the freezer, and keep bodies in the freezer until the grave is ready. Save graves for your own people and cremate raiders instead. With Ideology, a funeral needs the corpse in a grave or sarcophagus for full quality.
Visiting a grave counts as recreation, with a multiplier of 1 to 1.4, so add a sculpture for the colonists who come to visit.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: throne room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The size, impressiveness and furniture a noble's throne room needs at each title
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Build the throne room for the title your noble will hold next.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Titled nobles demand a throne room that grows with their rank: more area, more impressiveness and more furnishings at each title. A noble whose throne room falls short gets a mood penalty. Build it once with room to grow, so each promotion means adding furniture rather than knocking down walls. The plan comes as an audience chamber, a throne room and a grand throne room.

li.heading: What each title needs

table.li: Title | Area | Impressiveness | Furniture to add
Acolyte | 24 | - | a throne, every tile floored, 2 lit braziers, and a roof
Knight or Dame | 30 | 60 | 2 columns and a harp (a harpsichord or piano also counts)
Baron or Baroness | 60 | 120 | a grand throne, fine floors throughout, 2 drapes and a harpsichord (or piano)

li.after: A bestowing ceremony gets +40% quality in a room of impressiveness 170.

li.heading: Building it once
li.text:
Build big from the start. The throne room plan's 7x7 floor (49 tiles) covers titles up to Praetor; expand it for a Baron. Keep beds, workbenches and dining tables out, or the room stops counting, and check the Royalty tab for unmet requirements after every promotion.
Nobles also need a bedroom that suits their title and the right apparel; each missing apparel item costs -4 mood.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: temple
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A ritual room with an altar, lectern, seats and standing room for everyone
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Hold rituals in the temple; the room's impressiveness affects how they turn out.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Ideology rituals turn out better in an impressive room with the right furniture. A dedicated temple with an altar, a lectern and seating improves every ritual you hold there.

li.heading: What raises ritual quality

table.li: A room with impressiveness 120 | +20% for many rituals
6 speakers or 6 drums | +30% for dance and drum parties
A campfire | +20% for tribal drum parties

li.after: Keep a drum party's campfire on stone.

li.heading: What quality changes
li.text: Ritual quality isn't the chance of success, but it shifts the odds toward fun and unforgettable outcomes and away from terrible ones. At 50% quality the odds are about:

li.heading: Size and layout
li.text: Funerals, skylantern festivals and tree connections want 10 participants; trials want 20. Size the temple for your whole colony, standing and seated. Put the altar and lectern at one end, with seats facing them, and decorate for impressiveness with sculptures, fine floors and good light. Make it easy to reach, but don't route traffic through it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: classroom
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: School desks and blackboards where children learn from an adult
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Put the classroom where the adults already work.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Children learn skills faster at school desks, taught by an adult, and blackboards in the same room add to that. A classroom only works if a teacher is around, so put it where adults pass by and lessons actually happen.

li.heading: Desks, blackboards and a teacher
li.text:
A school desk is 2x1 and costs 30 material. Up to 3 blackboards count per desk, at +20% learning each, so link three to every desk: together they give 160% skill XP.
Lessons need an awake adult who is able to teach. Build the classroom near the adults' workplaces so a teacher is always close, keep it lit and warm, and add a toy box so children can play too.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: nursery
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A warm, safe room for cribs, close to the parents and far from the front door
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Put the cribs where a parent walks past every day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Babies sleep a lot, need regular feeding and can't move on their own, so their room should be warm, safe and close to whoever looks after them. A nursery keeps cribs out of the adults' bedrooms and gives the colony's youngest a room well away from the front door. The plan comes as a small nursery and a nursery with two cribs each, and a large nursery with four.

li.heading: Feeding
li.text: Babies need feeding twice a day. Baby food is cooked at a campfire or stove: 0.25 nutrition of vegetables makes 10 portions, and it rots in 14 days. Keep baby food or a feeding adult within easy reach of the cribs.

li.heading: Where the cribs go
li.text: Put the cribs in their own room near the parents' bedrooms. A bedroom with a child assigned stops counting as a bedroom unless a parent is assigned too. Keep the nursery warm, lit and away from the entrance, and add a toy box and a soft floor.

li.heading: Growth vats
li.text: A growth vat uses 200 W and 3 nutrition a day to age a child, or 6 a day to grow an embryo.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: brewery
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Fermenting barrels kept between 7 and 32 °C, near the hops field
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A barrel of wort today is beer in six days.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Beer is the simplest drug and a cheap mood lift, but fermenting barrels are fussy about temperature. A small roofed room beside the hops field and the storeroom keeps them in range all year. None of it needs power. The plan comes as a brew cellar of barrels, a brewery, and a large brewery with eight barrels.

li.heading: Keeping the barrels in range
li.text: Fermenting barrels only ferment between 7 and 32 °C, and a batch kept below -1 °C or above 32 °C for long is ruined. Insulate the room and keep it well inside the barrels' range, not close to either limit. Without power, a campfire warms it in winter and a passive cooler keeps it below 32 °C in summer.

li.heading: From hops to beer
li.text:
Hops take 5 listed growing days. Each barrel holds 25 wort and takes 6 days to ferment it. Put the brewery next to the hops field and the storeroom.
Beer carries a small risk of addiction with every bottle, so set a drug policy that lets it lift mood without becoming a habit.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: armory
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Weapons and armor on shelves near the defenses, far from the cells
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Store spare weapons where fighters pass on their way to the walls.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Spare weapons and armor on the floor clutter corridors; in an armory they're ready when the raid letter arrives. Put it between the bedrooms or barracks and the defensive line, where colonists can grab gear on the way, and keep it far from prison cells and slave quarters. The plan comes as a weapons locker, an armory and an arsenal.

li.text:
Weapons left outdoors deteriorate, so the armory needs a roof, a door and shelves, with weapons and armor sorted apart. Stored weapons and armor count toward colony wealth, and so toward raid size; sell or scrap weapons you'll never use.
The distance from slaves matters with Ideology: a usable weapon within 7 tiles of a slave, or in the same indoor room, makes rebellion 4 times as likely.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: battery room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Roofed, stone-floored, batteries in separate pairs, generators elsewhere
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Leave a gap between battery pairs, so one explosion doesn't set off the rest.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Batteries store power for the night and calm days, but unroofed batteries and bare conduits short out and start fires, and batteries packed together go up together. A plain stone room with a roof keeps one short circuit from taking out the colony's power and the rooms around it.

li.heading: Building it safely

points.li: Use stone floors and walls, roof every battery, and keep anything wooden out.
Build batteries in pairs, with a gap or a wall between each pair. Batteries packed together can chain-explode, so community players build them in separated pairs.
Use hidden conduits, and add a firefoam popper when you can.
Put generators in a separate room, with their fuel stored somewhere else.

li.after: Unroofed batteries and ordinary conduits can short-circuit; in recent versions, roofed batteries and hidden conduits prevent it.

li.heading: Storage and fuel
li.text: A battery stores 600 Wd and loses 5 Wd a day. A wood-fired generator burns 22 wood a day. A solar flare shuts down everything powered.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: crematorium
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: An electric crematorium in a small room beside the freezer
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Burn the raiders and bury your own.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: After a raid you'll have more bodies than graves. A crematorium burns them, so corpses stop lying in view and souring everyone's mood. The electric crematorium is industrial tech and needs power, so give it a small room of its own beside the freezer. Without power, use a graveyard instead.

li.heading: Bodies waiting their turn
li.text:
Seeing a corpse costs -4 mood and a rotting one -6, each for half a day. Rot stops at or below 0 °C, so bodies waiting in the freezer next door don't turn into rotting ones. Store them on a corpse-only stockpile in the freezer or a cold room next door until they're burned, and build the crematorium away from living space, so corpses aren't carried past the dining room.
Set a bill to cremate strangers' corpses and keep your own dead for graves.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: drug lab
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A drug lab bench in a clean, lit room beside the leaf and neutroamine store
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Decide what each colonist may take before the first batch is done.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The drug lab turns smokeleaf, psychoid leaves and neutroamine into recreational drugs, combat drugs and trade goods. The room itself is simple: put the bench next to where you store leaves and neutroamine, and keep it lit and clean like any workshop. What you make there needs drug policies to match, so set them before production starts, or the colony ends up with addicts. The plan has one bench or two.

li.heading: Recipes

table.li: Psychite tea | 400 | 4 psychoid leaves; needs Cooking 2

li.after: Colonies can't make neutroamine; it has to be bought or found. Spend it carefully, and keep go-juice and wake-up for emergencies.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: art studio
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: An art bench, good light and your best artist, making beauty for the whole base
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Put the best sculpture where the most people eat.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Sculptures are the most efficient way to make rooms beautiful and impressive, and their value multiplies with quality. An art studio gives your best artist a lit, clean place to work, near the storeroom. The best pieces then go where the most people see them: the dining room, the rec room and the hospital.

li.heading: Sculpture beauty
li.after: Sculpture beauty is (base x material modifier + material offset) x quality; good quality doubles it, legendary multiplies it by 8. The material offset counts once per sculpture, so four large legendary gold sculptures (13,440) beat one grand one (12,960).

li.heading: The artist
li.text: Give art only to your best artist; low-quality pieces waste material. The art bench is neolithic tech, so tribes can use it. With Ideology, slaves can't do art.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: meditation room
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A quiet, beautiful room where psycasters meditate for psyfocus
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Put the meditation spot in a room people don't walk through.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Psycasters regain psyfocus by meditating, and what's around them matters, depending on their focus types. A quiet, beautiful room off the main corridors, with a meditation spot, keeps them out of the traffic and away from noise. Meditation counts as recreation too.

li.heading: Furnishing for the focus

table.li: Focus type | What to put near the spot
Void (Anomaly) | a holding platform or holding spot, which works as a cheap void meditation focus anywhere

li.after: With Anomaly, check an entity's containment before meditating beside its platform.

li.heading: Meditation time
li.text: Schedule meditation time so psyfocus is full before you need it. Royal meditation and prayer count as recreation, at a 1x multiplier. Go-juice gives +15% psyfocus; wake-up gives +20% meditation speed.
